To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the coexistence of two species in a spatially extended model for dryland plant communities is facilitated by strong competition between individuals of one species only, which has a stronger dispersal ability and higher fitness than its competitor.

the coexistence of grasses and trees in dryland vegetation patterns is facilitated by intraspecies competition of one species and that this competition leads to the observed species distribution within vegetation bands.

(i) coexistence is facilitated if the locally superior species has a lower average fitness, (ii) coexistence can be explained without making assumptions about differences in species dispersal behaviour, and (iii) spatial patterns in dryland vegetation can be explained by differences in species’ dispersal behaviour.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interplay between species’ dispersal and local competition and its impact on the coexistence of species.

the question of how species coexistence is facilitated under competition for a limiting resource and provides new insights into how intraspecific competition can enable coexistence of competing species.
the question how species diversity can arise in the face of strong competition and how it is maintained.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
intraspecific competition is a crucial mechanism that facilitates coexistence of species in dryland vegetation patterns.

the spatially extended model is able to explain the coexistence of species with contrasting dispersal behaviours and that the coexistence of these species is facilitated by strong competition of one species.
intraspecific competition is an essential mechanism that facilitates species coexistence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
intraspecific competition can be a major driver in coexistence of two plant species, but that spatial self-organisation is crucial for the observed spatial species distributions.
species coexistence can be explained by the interplay of interspecific and intrispecific competition without relying on strong assumptions about the differences between the two species.
the coexistence of two plant species is facilitated by intraspecies competition of the superior competitor species.
The main takeaway from our work is that
intraspecific dynamics can be as relevant as interspecific dynamics in explaining species coexistence.
intraspecific competition can facilitate the coexistence of two species without relying on assumptions about differences in their dispersal or functional response to the limiting resource.
the interplay of interspecific and intracpecific competition in spatially explicit models can facilitate the coexistence of competing species.
